videos.title: Verify bytes before trusting events
videos.description:
A webhook's successful response should mean durable acceptance, not completed business work.

Stripe signs the request body, so preserve the original bytes and verify them with the signature header and endpoint secret. An invalid signature leaves the business path immediately.

This diagram proposes a durable inbox after verification. Commit the payload and event ID before returning success; a known duplicate reuses that receipt. If storage fails, do not acknowledge a receipt you cannot recover.

An asynchronous worker then claims pending events and records the local state update with its completion marker. Failed work retries the pending receipt. External side effects still require their own idempotency contract, and distinct events can need domain-level deduplication too.

Transport acceptance, business completion and replay safety are separate boundaries. Event delivery order is not a promise.

When your endpoint returns 2xx, what exactly can you recover after a crash?

#APIDesign #Webhooks #ReliabilityEngineering

videos.title: Caching moves the freshness bill
videos.description:
A cache write policy decides who pays for freshness and when a write is acknowledged.

This map compares three alternatives, with no flow between them. Cache-aside writes the database first and then invalidates the cached copy. That keeps the write path relatively simple, but misses and stale-read windows still need attention.

Write-through coordinates the database and cache updates before acknowledgement. It trades extra write latency and partial-failure handling for fresher reads on that managed path; it does not make separate stores one atomic transaction.

Write-behind acknowledges before the database catches up. Faster acknowledgement creates a pending-write recovery problem, so protecting that backlog matters more than the cache label.

The moving signals stay inside each strategy. Read paths are omitted to keep the comparison focused on write responsibility.

Which matters more for your workload: acknowledgement latency, immediate freshness or recovery after a failed flush?

#SystemDesign #Caching #DataEngineering

videos.title: A queue buys time, not capacity
videos.description:
A queue absorbs a burst; it cannot fix a permanently overloaded database.

For background jobs, put durable storage between admission and processing, then cap the consumers' aggregate downstream rate. Adding workers without that cap can simply move the overload from the queue to the database.

Watch the oldest pending job as well as queue depth. Sustained arrivals above the safe processing rate mean increasing delay, even when every component is healthy. Bound admission, scale within the dependency's limits, or explicitly shed work.

The diagram separates job delivery, successful-commit acknowledgement and operational feedback. Consumers still need idempotent handling because delivery can repeat. Persistent failures belong in a dead-letter path with diagnosis before resubmission.

What signal tells you to stop accepting work before your queue becomes tomorrow's incident?

#SystemDesign #DistributedSystems #ReliabilityEngineering

共享文件、细小措辞、优化程序和交接状态看似都在模型外，却直接决定协作成本、控制风险、算法入口和执行可靠性。能力进了系统，成本和风险也就藏进接口里。
